This paper introduces the TARMA model, a novel framework that integrates the seasonal and temporal-variable components of ARIMA models with a simple linear model to model the temporal-varying Poisson autoregressive component. Furthermore, we apply the TARMA model to daily stock price data for the IBM company to illustrate its practical utility. The results indicate that the simple linear component can capture strong nonlinear nonlinear temporal variations and provide accurate forecasts. The applied example also confirms that the TARMA model outperforms other models in terms of forecasting accuracy. Finally, we suggest several potential directions for future research. Current automatic image description models are evaluated using intrinsic evaluation metrics that involve comparing the generated description $D$ with a human reference $R$ to calculate an similarity score. Ideally, a single-intrinsically high-scoring description should be deemed valid by a human reader. However, there is a significant gap between the expectations of intrinsic evaluation metrics and actual human reference usage; readers often perform "reference-based reading," utilizing the human reference to understand and judge the generated output. To bridge this gap, we should optimize image description models directly for how humans use references. In this work, we introduce a learning framework for image descriptions that leverages human references, treating them as a form of supervision. Specifically, we propose a neural model called Attractive Score (AttrScore), which regresses an attractive score based on the joint embedding of the image and its caption, to guide regression-based image description generation. Using this approach, we demonstrate that when optimized for AttrScore, our model produces descriptions that align better with human preferences than those from state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, we introduce an editing task, showing that AttrScore can assist in generating descriptions that satisfy specific constraints. To support these tasks, we created a dataset of 117K multilingual references from FreeImageDescrptions.com and conducted extensive evaluations. Our findings indicate that AttrScore effectively predicts human preferences across different intrinsic metrics and reference sources, and that descriptions edited via AttrScore are more likely to meet users' constraints. The code for AttrScore and the dataset will be made available at https://github.com/soham9186/AttrScore and https://github.com/soham9186/AttrScore-desr.

This presentation reports on selected LHC experiments involving small systems, ranging from cosmic rays to future colliders. We begin by detailing the air shower technique used to study cosmic rays, highlighting the record-setters: the Auger and GLAST telescopes. We then examine the ALICE experiment's investigation of quark-gluon plasma in heavy ion collisions, and we outline small system studies at LHC energies, including proton-proton, proton-nucleus, and light ion collisions. Finally, we discuss upcoming small system research at the LHC and at future colliders. The accompanying talk by A. Capelest will cover some of these same topics. These investigations will be continued at the LHC by the smaller, specialized "LHCf" experiment and by the CLAS12 experiment at Jefferson Lab in the US, and by the FASER$\gamma$ experiment at the LHC. We will also explore studies of small systems at the Electron-Ion Collider and at 10 TeV proton-proton collisions at the Future Circular Collider. These investigations aim to explore hadronic physics beyond the quark-gluon plasma in small systems and address "hierarchy" problems at both hadronic and lepton colliders. We will provide an update on these studies at the 2019 Quark Gluon Plasma conference. Starting with low-energy cosmic rays, we will describe the related experiments and literature, presenting initial estimates for feasible experiments at high energies. We will focus on multiplicity as a key observable for high-energy physics, noting that the "maximum multiplicity per unit rapidity" ($M_{uv}$) has served as a record-setter in cosmic ray physics (see Fig. 1). The variable emission from X-ray binaries near the Galactic Centre, specifically the presence or absence of transient outbursts over decades, is utilized to examine the Carus-Andronico conjecture regarding stellar collapse. This variable activity is also applied to characterize the dormant systems in the same region. While the general relativistic theory of collapse depends on the initial conditions of a specific star's density distribution, the Andronico-Carus conjecture posits that a neutron star's ability to halt its contraction during a transient event is contingent upon the uniformity of that distribution. Consequently, we analyze the timescales required for a neutron star in a transient binary to reach a new gravitational equilibrium, referred to as the "repetition interval." An examination of the repetition intervals for five of these stars reveals that Millisecond Pulsars in the Galactic Centre represent a distinct category from other systems. Ultimately, the Carus-Andronico conjecture is rejected. Finally, the potential utility of these systems as precise clocks for navigating the densely populated Galactic Centre is discussed. Evaluating the security protocols of high-value protocols like TLS is crucial, as these protocols are subjected to intense cryptographic analysis to identify potential vulnerabilities. However, such audits are often hindered by the high performance requirements needed for effective attacks, which fall outside the capabilities of standard-off-the-shelf (SOTR) hardware. Among the most critical hyperparameters for neural networks, the loss function plays a pivotal role, yet selecting the appropriate one remains challenging. Despite the availability of numerous loss functions, related works often fail to provide sufficient justification for their specific choice. This study conducts an in-depth comparison of popular loss functions—MSE, MAE, KL, CE, and a combination of MSE and CE—across both simulated and real-world datasets. Furthermore, we observe that certain functions, specifically MSE and the combined MSE+CE, tend to overfit more easily than others. Guided by these results, we anticipate that adopting the KL loss function will further enhance the accuracy of networks utilizing the knowledge distillation approach. To support this, we implemented it within a pre-trained knowledge distillation model. Ultimately, this research highlights that loss function selection should be driven by the specific characteristics of the dataset and the desired objectives, rather than adopted arbitrarily. A graph $G=(V,E)$ equipped with a metric $d$ constitutes a metric space, where the metric is defined by the shortest path distance between vertices. The metric dimension of $G$, denoted as $\dim(G)$, is the smallest number of vertices required to form a resolving set based on the distance metric $d$. This paper introduces the concept of shortened metric dimension, $\dim_s(G)$, defined by the optimized metric $d_s$, which limits the distance between any two vertices to one. This concept aligns with the asymptotic metric used in Lipschitz algebra. Consequently, the shortened metric dimension can be determined using a resolved tree with the graph's diameter as its depth. We establish that $\dim_s(G) \leq \dim(G)$ and provide methods to calculate both the traditional and shortened metric dimensions. Specifically, we demonstrate that $\dim_s(G)$ can be derived from $G$'s diameter and its vertices' degrees, whereas $\dim(G)$ can be computed from its diameter, degrees, and edges. Finally, we confirm that $\dim_s(G)$ depends solely on $G$'s diameter, degrees, and edges. Notably, we present an example where $\dim_s(G)$ is significantly lower than $\dim(G)$. Additionally, we derive the exact values for $\dim_s(G)$ and $\dim(G)$ across various standard graph families.

By and large, massive galaxies tend to be quiescent, whereas lower-mass galaxies are predominantly star-forming; consequently, specific star-forming rates (sSFR) peak at $M^{\ast}$ and decline for both lower and higher masses. While central densities of quiescent galaxies exceed those of star-forming ones at similar masses, the specific central star-forming rates (sSFR_c) of the latter are consistently low across all masses. This study introduces a novel data-driven inverse approach based on a physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework to reconstruct loading conditions from vibration responses. Unlike traditional regularization techniques, the proposed PINN method integrates key physical constraints directly into the optimization process: conservation of energy through a weak form of the equation of motion, one-way coupling of the acoustic field, and a linear relationship between structural displacement and acoustic pressure. These integrations enable the simultaneous reconstruction of both acoustic and structural loading conditions. Validation is performed on a simply supported plate subjected to random loading under free boundary conditions, as well as on a plate with clamped-conical boundaries exposed to plane wave incidence. The results demonstrate that the data-driven PINN strategy successfully recovers both the magnitude and spatial distribution of the loading, confirming its effectiveness as a reliable alternative to conventional regularization approaches. Furthermore, the method's utility in identifying unknown boundary conditions and detecting sudden loading events is illustrated through two additional examples.
